samples.question: The picture shows one long black horizontal axis with short ticks along its lower edge, and four bent rods drawn above it: one red, one green, one blue and one orange, each in its own horizontal lane. Every rod is a single bent line made of two straight pieces joined at a corner, and all four rods are drawn with the same thickness. Imagine the light falling straight down the page, so that every point of a rod drops vertically onto the axis. The stretch of axis that a rod darkens in this way is its SHADOW, and the width of that stretch is what has to be compared: it runs from the leftmost point anywhere on the rod to the rightmost point anywhere on the rod. The corner counts as part of the rod, so a rod that doubles back casts a shadow wider than the gap between its two loose ends, and for such a rod the two ends are the wrong things to measure. Nothing else about a rod matters: not how long the bent line itself is, not how much ink it uses, not how steeply it climbs, not how tall its lane is, not which lane it lies in and not how far left or right it sits. The rod that is drawn longest, the rod whose two ends are farthest apart, the topmost rod and the bottom rod are each the answer only as often as chance allows. Which rod casts the widest shadow on the axis? Answer red, green, blue or orange.
